title: Burning smell
h1: Why does my car smell like something is burning?
metaDesc: Burning smell from your car? Answer a few quick questions to see possible causes, how urgent it may be, and what to tell your mechanic.
synonyms: car smells like something is burning
burning smell when heater is on
intro: A burning smell can be as minor as dust on the heater or as serious as an electrical fault. The type of smell and whether there's smoke give strong clues. Answer a few questions to see how urgent it may be and what might be burning.
safety: If you see smoke or flames, pull over, turn off the engine, get everyone out and move well away from the car. Call 911 from a safe spot, even if you can't see flames.
If you smell burning plastic or hot wiring, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the temperature gauge is in the red, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the brake pedal feels soft or the brakes fade after a burning smell near a wheel, stop as soon as it's safe.

q_danger.q: Is there any smoke, or is a warning light or the temperature gauge telling you something's wrong?

opts.a: Yes, there's smoke from under the hood or around a wheel
The temperature gauge is high, or a red warning light is on
No smoke and no warning lights
I'm not sure

q_type.help: Smells are easiest to tell apart right after you stop. Step out and sniff near the hood and each wheel.

opts.a: Burning oil: sharp and acrid, like a hot frying pan
Burning rubber, or hot brakes (often described as burning carpet)
Burning plastic or hot wiring
Sweet, like syrup or maple
A burnt, acrid smell while the clutch slips on a manual car
I'm not sure

q_rubber.q: When and where do you notice it?

opts.a: Near one wheel, and that wheel is much hotter than the others or the car pulls to one side
After going down a long hill, towing, or a lot of hard braking
From the engine, along with a squeal when starting or turning
Under the car, like something got caught on the exhaust
I'm not sure
From the vents, the first few times I use the heat this season
Near one wheel after driving
From the hood after I park
After an oil change or other engine work in the last few days
I'm not sure

result.title: Something is hot enough to smoke. Treat it as a fire risk
result.now: If you see smoke and think your car may be on fire, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn off the engine. Get everyone out. Leave the hood closed. Move at least 100 feet from the car and stay away from traffic. Call 911 from a safe spot, even if you can't see flames.
if: If the smoke stops once the engine is off and you can see it was oil or coolant on a hot part, it still needs repair before the car is used again.
If the smoke is at a wheel, the brake may be stuck on. Don't touch the wheel. It can be extremely hot.
If the brake pedal felt soft or the car was harder to stop, tell the tow driver and the shop.
result.why: Smoke usually means oil, coolant, plastic or a brake part is burning or boiling. Any of those can turn into a fire, and it's impossible to tell how bad it is while driving.

causes.name: Oil or fluid leaking onto the exhaust
causes.clues: Blue-gray smoke from under the hood with a burning oil smell.

causes.name: Coolant boiling over
causes.clues: White, sweet-smelling steam, often with a high temperature gauge.

causes.name: Brake stuck on
causes.clues: Smoke at one wheel, and that wheel is very hot.

causes.name: Electrical short
causes.clues: Burning plastic smell, sometimes with a blown fuse or dead accessories.

shop: Engine bay inspection for leaks and burn marks

result.title: The engine may be overheating or losing oil
result.now: Pull over safely and turn off the engine. Don't drive it. Have it towed, or call roadside assistance (your insurer, a motor club, or the number in your owner's manual).
if: If the oil pressure light was on, don't restart the engine. It can be destroyed within minutes without oil pressure.
Never open the radiator or coolant cap while the engine is hot.
If you see steam or smoke from under the hood, step away from the car and don't open the hood until it has cooled.
result.why: A burning smell with a high temperature reading or a red warning light can mean the engine is in trouble right now. Overheating and low oil pressure both cause serious damage quickly.

causes.name: Coolant leak and overheating
causes.clues: A sweet smell, steam, or the temperature gauge in the red.

causes.name: Very low engine oil
causes.clues: The oil pressure light is on and you smell burning oil.

causes.name: Charging system fault
causes.clues: The battery light is on, with a burning rubber or electrical smell.

you: Once the engine is fully cold, check the oil and coolant levels.
shop: Code scan and charging system check

result.title: Oil may be dripping onto the hot exhaust
result.now: Pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off and let it cool. Oil on a hot exhaust can catch fire. Once it's cool, check the oil level. Don't drive it again until the source of the leak has been found. Have it towed, or have a mechanic look at it where it's parked.
if: If you see smoke from under the hood, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the oil is below the lowest mark on the dipstick, don't drive it until it's topped up.
If the car just had an oil change, a little spilled oil may be burning off. That often fades within a few drives. If it doesn't, have the shop that did the work recheck it.
If the oil pressure light comes on or the temperature gauge rises, pull over and turn off the engine.
result.why: A burning oil smell often comes from a small leak above the exhaust. The oil cooks on hot metal and the smell comes into the cabin through the vents. A gasket is a common source, and leaks tend to get worse. A shop will usually confirm the source before replacing anything.

causes.name: Leaking valve cover gasket
causes.clues: Oily residue on top of the engine, with the smell strongest after a drive.

causes.name: Spilled oil from a recent oil change
causes.clues: The smell started right after an oil change and is fading.

causes.name: Loose oil filter, drain plug or filler cap
causes.clues: Fresh drips under the car or oil sprayed around the filler cap.

you: Look for oily residue on top of the engine and drips under the car.
shop: Dye test if the source isn't clear

result.title: A burning plastic smell may be an electrical short
result.now: Pull over, turn off the engine and don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mechanic check it where it's parked.
if: If you see smoke or flames, get everyone out and at least 100 feet away from the car and call 911.

If you find a plastic bag stuck on the exhaust and the smell is completely gone once it's removed (with everything cool), an electrical fault is less likely. If the smell returns, have the car checked before driving it.
result.why: Burning plastic or hot wiring can mean a wire, connector or electrical part is overheating. That can melt insulation and start a fire, so it's not something to drive on.

causes.name: Shorted or overheating wiring
causes.clues: A sharp electrical smell, blown fuses, or things that stop working.

causes.name: Failing blower motor or resistor
causes.clues: The smell comes from the vents and the fan acts strangely or only works on some speeds.

causes.name: Plastic stuck on the exhaust
causes.clues: The smell is strongest outside, under the car.

causes.name: Aftermarket accessory wiring
causes.clues: A recently added stereo, lights, charger or dash cam.

you: Once the car is off and cool, look under the car for plastic stuck to the exhaust.
shop: Electrical inspection for melted wiring or connectors

result.title: A sweet smell often points to a coolant leak
result.now: Check the coolant overflow tank level when the engine is cold, top it up if needed, and get it checked within a few days. Watch your temperature gauge.
if: If the temperature gauge rises above normal, pull over and turn off the engine.
If the smell is strong inside the car or the windshield fogs with a greasy film, the heater core may be leaking. Keep the windows cracked, and don't drive if the windshield fogs and won't clear.
If you see steam from under the hood, or the coolant level drops again quickly after topping up, don't drive it until it's checked.
result.why: Coolant has a sweet, syrupy smell when it hits hot engine parts. Even a small leak can drain the system over time and lead to overheating.

causes.name: Leaking radiator hose or clamp
causes.clues: Crusty residue on a hose, or drips under the front of the car.

causes.name: Leaking heater core
causes.clues: The smell is strongest inside, with a damp passenger carpet or foggy windshield.

causes.name: Water pump or radiator leak
causes.clues: Drips at the front of the engine or under the radiator.

you: Check the coolant level when cold.
Look for drips or crusty residue around hoses.

result.title: The clutch may be overheating, often from slipping or riding it
result.now: Take your foot fully off the clutch pedal while driving and avoid slipping it on hills. Book a check if the smell comes back without heavy use.
if: If the engine revs rise but the car doesn't speed up, the clutch is slipping. Get it checked within a few days.
If the smell came from one hard hill start or getting unstuck, let it cool. It may be a one-off.
If you see smoke from under the car or it won't move in gear, stop and have it towed.
result.why: A clutch works by friction. Slipping it, riding the pedal or a worn clutch makes heat, and the friction material gives off a sharp burnt smell.

causes.name: Driving habits (riding or slipping the clutch)
causes.clues: It happens on hill starts, in heavy traffic or when towing.

causes.name: Worn clutch
causes.clues: The engine revs up without the car speeding up, especially in higher gears.

causes.name: Oil on the clutch from a leak
causes.clues: Oil drips where the engine meets the transmission.

you: On a quiet, safe road, in a high gear at low speed, press the gas firmly once. If the revs jump but the car doesn't speed up, the clutch is slipping. Don't repeat it, since each try adds heat.
shop: Leak check at the rear main seal

result.title: A brake may be stuck on and dragging
result.now: Pull over and let it cool. Don't touch the wheel. Have it towed, or call roadside assistance (your insurer, a motor club, or the number in your owner's manual).
if: If the parking brake was left on, release it and let the brakes cool. Even if the smell and pull go away, overheated brakes can be weakened, so have them checked before relying on the car.
If you see smoke at the wheel, stand well back.
If the brake pedal feels soft, sinks, or the red brake light is on, don't move the car.
result.why: When a brake doesn't release, it keeps rubbing and gets extremely hot. That can make the brakes fade, damage the parts, and in bad cases start a fire.

causes.name: Sticking brake caliper
causes.clues: One wheel much hotter than the others and the car pulls to that side.

causes.name: Parking brake not fully released
causes.clues: The smell comes from the rear wheels, or the parking brake light is on.

causes.name: Collapsed brake hose
causes.clues: The drag comes and goes, and the caliper looks fine.

you: Make sure the parking brake is fully released.

result.title: Your brakes may have overheated from heavy use
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe, set the parking brake and let the brakes cool for at least 30 minutes. Have the brakes and brake fluid checked before relying on them again, especially for a long drive or another hill.
if: If the pedal felt soft, sank, or the brakes faded, don't drive on after they cool. Have them checked before driving further.
If the smell comes back during normal driving, a brake may be dragging. Get it checked soon.
If you see smoke from a wheel, one wheel stays much hotter than the others, or the car pulls to one side, a brake may be dragging. Don't drive further until it's checked.
result.why: Long downhill braking or towing can heat brake pads past their comfort zone, and they give off a sharp smell. It often goes away once they cool, but very hot brakes don't stop as well, and repeated overheating can damage the pads, rotors and fluid.

causes.name: Brakes overheated on a long descent or while towing
causes.clues: The smell appeared after a long hill or a heavy load.

causes.name: New pads still bedding in
causes.clues: The brakes were just replaced.

causes.name: Dragging brake
causes.clues: One wheel hotter than the others, even after normal driving.

you: Once cool, press the pedal. If it feels soft or sinks, don't drive it. A firm pedal is a good sign, but it isn't proof the brakes weren't damaged.
After a normal drive, carefully hold your hand near each wheel (without touching) to see if one is much hotter.

result.title: A slipping drive belt may be causing the burning rubber smell
result.now: With the engine off, look at the belt for cracks, glazing or fraying, and get it checked within a few days.
if: If the battery light comes on, the steering gets heavy or the temperature rises, pull over and turn off the engine. The belt may have broken. Have it towed.
If the belt is visibly frayed or missing pieces, don't drive it until it's checked.
result.why: The drive belt runs the alternator, power steering and often the water pump. When it slips on a pulley it heats up and smells like burning rubber. A stuck pulley or a weak tensioner is often behind it, so a shop will usually check those before replacing the belt.

causes.name: Worn or loose drive belt
causes.clues: A squeal at startup or when turning the wheel, and a shiny, cracked belt.

causes.name: Seized or dragging pulley
causes.clues: A pulley that grinds or won't spin freely.

causes.name: Weak belt tensioner
causes.clues: The belt flutters or jumps while the engine runs.

you: With the engine off, look at the belt for cracks and shiny, glazed sides.

result.title: Something may be stuck on the hot exhaust
result.now: Once the car has cooled for at least 30 minutes, look under the car along the exhaust for a plastic bag, leaves or other debris and carefully remove it.
if: If you can't reach it or it's melted on, have a shop remove it.
If the smell continues with nothing stuck there, get it checked within a few days.
If you see smoke and think the car may be on fire, get everyone out, leave the hood closed, move at least 100 feet away and call 911, even if you can't see flames.
result.why: Plastic bags, road debris and leaves can wrap around the exhaust and melt or smolder. It smells alarming, but once it's removed the smell usually goes away.

causes.name: Plastic bag or debris on the exhaust
causes.clues: The smell is strongest outside the car, under the middle.

causes.name: Leaves under the heat shield
causes.clues: You recently parked on or drove through leaves.

causes.name: Fluid leak onto the exhaust
causes.clues: Oily residue or drips near the exhaust.

you: With the exhaust cool, look along it for debris.

result.title: It may be dust burning off the heater
result.now: Run the heat on high for a few minutes with a window cracked. If it's dust, the smell usually fades within minutes.
if: If the smell lasts more than a day or two of use, or smells like plastic, have the blower motor and wiring checked.
If the smell is sweet or the windshield fogs, it may be a heater core leak. Check your coolant level.
If you see smoke from the vents or dash, pull over, turn off the engine and get out.
result.why: Dust settles on the heating parts over the summer. The first few times you use the heat, it can burn off with a brief, dusty smell. That's common and normally fades quickly.

causes.name: Dust on the heater parts
causes.clues: First use of the season, and the smell fades in minutes.

causes.name: Dirty cabin air filter
causes.clues: Weak airflow and a musty or dusty smell.

causes.name: Failing blower motor or resistor
causes.clues: A plastic or electrical smell, or the fan only works on some speeds.

you: Check whether the smell fades after a few minutes.
Look at the cabin air filter (your owner's manual shows where).

result.title: Hard to pin down without a look. Get it checked within a few days
result.now: Check your oil and coolant levels when the engine is cool, look under the car for drips or debris, and get it checked within a few days.
if: If you see smoke or the smell becomes plastic-like or electrical, pull over and turn off the engine.
If a warning light comes on or the temperature gauge rises, stop driving it.
result.why: Burning smells come from oil, coolant, brakes, belts, the clutch or wiring. A technician can usually find the source quickly by looking for leaks, hot spots and burn marks.

causes.name: Oil leaking onto the exhaust
causes.clues: The smell is strongest at the hood after a drive.

causes.name: Dragging brake
causes.clues: The smell is near one wheel.

causes.name: Slipping belt
causes.clues: A squeal from the engine.

you: Note when the smell happens and where it's strongest.
Check the oil and coolant levels.
